text: Section 43A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 imposes an obligation on body corporates to implement reasonable security practices to protect sensitive personal data.
Section 66 of the IT Act deals with computer-related offences and provides for punishment of up to 3 years imprisonment or a fine of up to one lakh rupees.
Section 66A of the IT Act was struck down by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.
Section 69 of the IT Act empowers the Central Government to issue directions for interception, monitoring, or decryption of any information through any computer resource.
Section 67 of the IT Act punishes publication or transmission of obscene material in electronic form.

Section 72 of the IT Act provides for breach of confidentiality and privacy where any person who, in pursuance of any of the powers conferred under the Act, secures access to any electronic record or information, discloses the same without consent, is punishable.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides a safe harbour for intermediaries from liability for third-party content provided they comply with due diligence requirements.
The right to privacy is a fundamental right under the Constitution of India, as held by the Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India.
Section 66E of the IT Act penalises the violation of privacy by capturing, publishing, or transmitting the image of a private area of any person without their consent.
Section 66C of the IT Act punishes identity theft — the fraudulent or dishonest use of the electronic signature, password, or any other unique identification feature of another person.
Section 66D of the IT Act punishes cheating by personation using a computer resource.
Section 66B of the IT Act punishes dishonest receipt of stolen computer resource or communication device.
Section 43 of the IT Act provides that if any person without permission of the owner accesses, downloads, or introduces a computer virus, he shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation.
The Information Technology (Amendment) Act was enacted in 2008.
Section 70 of the IT Act deals with protected systems and empowers the appropriate government to declare any computer resource as a protected system.
The Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.
In Miranda v. Arizona (1966), the Supreme Court held that suspects must be informed of their rights before custodial interrogation.
In Gideon v. Wainwright (1963), the Supreme Court held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment.
In Mapp v. Ohio (1961), the Supreme Court applied the exclusionary rule to the states, holding that evidence obtained through unconstitutional searches cannot be used in state court.
In Terry v. Ohio (1968), the Supreme Court held that police may conduct a brief investigatory stop and pat-down frisk if they have reasonable articulable suspicion of criminal activity.
42 U.S.C. Section 1983 provides a civil cause of action for persons whose federal constitutional or statutory rights have been violated by someone acting under color of state law.
In Roe v. Wade (1973), the Supreme Court recognized a constitutional right to abortion under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Supreme Court held that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution protects against self-incrimination and double jeopardy, and contains the Takings Clause.
Section 67A of the IT Act punishes publishing or transmitting material containing sexually explicit acts in electronic form.
Section 67B of the IT Act specifically penalises material depicting children in sexually explicit acts.
Section 66F of the IT Act defines and punishes cyber terrorism, including acts that threaten unity, integrity, or security of India.
Section 72A of the IT Act punishes disclosure of information in breach of lawful contract.
Section 69A of the IT Act empowers the government to block public access to any information through any computer resource in the interest of sovereignty or security of India.
Section 69B of the IT Act empowers the government to authorise any agency to monitor and collect traffic data or information for cyber security.
The Supreme Court of India upheld Aadhaar in the Puttaswamy II judgment but struck down its use for private entities.
In Alabama v. White (1990), the Supreme Court held that an anonymous tip, sufficiently corroborated, may provide reasonable suspicion for an investigatory stop.
Section 43 of the IT Act applies to damage caused to any computer, computer system, or computer network by a person acting without the permission of the owner.
Cyber Appellate Tribunal is established under Section 48 of the Information Technology Act, 2000.
Section 85 of the IT Act holds directors and officers of companies liable for offences committed by the company if the offence was committed with their consent, connivance, or negligence.
The exclusionary rule prevents unconstitutionally obtained evidence from being used in a criminal trial.
The Sixth Amendment guarantees the right to a speedy and public trial by an impartial jury.
Section 43A imposes liability on body corporates handling sensitive personal data for negligent data security practices that cause wrongful loss or gain.
In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act as unconstitutional for being vague and overbroad, violating the right to free speech.
Sections 65 and 66 of the IT Act were part of the original Information Technology Act, 2000 before the 2008 Amendment.
In Escobedo v. Illinois (1964), the Supreme Court held that a suspect has the right to consult with an attorney during police interrogation.
Section 78 of the IT Act empowers the police to investigate offences under the Act, with a Deputy Superintendent of Police being the minimum rank for investigation of most IT Act offences.
The due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment prohibits states from depriving any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law.
The IT Act 2000 received Presidential assent on 9 June 2000.
The right against self-incrimination under the Fifth Amendment means a person cannot be compelled to be a witness against themselves in a criminal case.
Section 65 of the IT Act punishes tampering with computer source documents.
In Katz v. United States (1967), the Supreme Court held that the Fourth Amendment protects people, not places, and introduced the reasonable expectation of privacy doctrine.
Section 43A mandates that body corporates implement the IS/ISO/IEC 27001 standard or an equivalent standard as their information security practices.
Section 79 safe harbour protection does not apply if the intermediary has conspired or abetted the unlawful act.
The Supreme Court in Puttaswamy I (2017) overruled the earlier decisions in M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh that held there was no fundamental right to privacy.
Section 43A of the IT Act requires data controllers to obtain explicit written consent from users before collecting sensitive personal data or information.
Section 43 of the IT Act provides for criminal punishment of up to 5 years for unauthorized access to a computer system.
In Miranda v. Arizona (1984), the Supreme Court ruled that suspects must be read their rights.
Section 66A of the IT Act is still in force and penalises offensive online speech.
Section 72 of the IT Act imposes criminal liability only on government officials who breach confidentiality, not private employees.
42 U.S.C. Section 1983 requires a plaintiff to prove that the defendant acted with actual malice.
The Fourth Amendment requires police to obtain a warrant before conducting any search or seizure.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides absolute immunity to intermediaries for all third-party content.
Gideon v. Wainwright held that the right to counsel applies only to felony cases in federal court.
Section 66C of the IT Act punishes the hacking of computer systems and carries a penalty of up to 10 years imprisonment.
The Supreme Court's exclusionary rule was established in Weeks v. United States for state courts.
Section 67 of the IT Act requires the government to prove actual harm to public morality to obtain a conviction.
The right to privacy declared in Puttaswamy is an absolute fundamental right that cannot be restricted by any law.
Section 43A applies to government bodies that handle sensitive personal data of citizens.
The Miranda warning must be given in all police encounters, including routine traffic stops.
Section 66A was struck down because it violated the right to equality under Article 14 of the Constitution.
In Terry v. Ohio, the court required probable cause for an investigatory stop.
Section 69 of the IT Act requires a court order before the government can intercept any electronic communication.
Section 70A of the IT Act established the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) as the national nodal agency for cybersecurity.
The Fourteenth Amendment to the US Constitution was enacted in 1870 to grant voting rights to freed slaves.
Section 43A of the IT Act may impose an obligation on body corporates to compensate individuals whose data was compromised.
Certain provisions of the IT Act could potentially conflict with international data protection frameworks like GDPR.
Courts have generally interpreted Section 79 of the IT Act narrowly to limit safe harbour protections.
The privacy ruling in Puttaswamy may eventually lead to a comprehensive data protection law in India.
Section 43A could be used to hold social media companies liable for data breaches affecting Indian users.
Miranda rights may not need to be given if the suspect spontaneously confesses.
The IT Act's provisions on data protection are considered inadequate compared to modern standards.
Section 66F cyber terrorism provisions have been used in several high-profile cases in India.
The balance between national security and privacy under the IT Act remains unsettled in Indian courts.
Section 79 safe harbour may be interpreted differently by courts depending on the specific content type involved.
Whether Section 43A applies to foreign companies processing Indian citizens' data extraterritorially is unclear.
Fourth Amendment protections might extend to digital data stored in cloud services under certain circumstances.
The scope of Section 66's punishments may vary depending on judicial interpretation of 'dishonest' intent.
Intermediaries under the IT Act may need to retain user data for investigation purposes under government orders.
The Miranda decision might apply differently in the context of digital evidence collection.
Section 43A of the IT Act may be supplemented by sector-specific data protection regulations in certain industries.
Whether Section 66A's invalidation creates a legal vacuum for online speech regulation in India is debated.
Section 79 of the IT Act may offer a defence to e-commerce platforms for user-generated product reviews.
The proportionality test under the Puttaswamy framework requires any privacy restriction to be narrowly tailored.
Section 66B of the IT Act punishes the act of publishing obscene material online.
In Katz v. United States (1967), Justice Harlan's concurrence established the two-part reasonable expectation of privacy test.
Section 43 of the IT Act provides both civil compensation remedies and criminal penalties.
The Fifth Amendment's protection against self-incrimination was extended to state proceedings in Malloy v. Hogan (1964).
Section 69A blocking orders issued by the government can be challenged before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution.
The 'reasonable articulable suspicion' standard from Terry v. Ohio is lower than the 'probable cause' standard required for an arrest warrant.
Section 43A of the IT Act imposes strict liability on body corporates regardless of their negligence.
The IT Act 2000 was the first comprehensive legislation on e-commerce and cybercrime in India.
The CERT-In established under Section 70B of the IT Act has the power to issue directions to service providers, intermediaries, and data centres for cybersecurity compliance.
The Cyber Appellate Tribunal under the IT Act hears appeals against orders of the Controller of Certifying Authorities.
Section 43A liability requires both proof of a data breach and proof that the body corporate failed to implement reasonable security practices.
Miranda v. Arizona (1966) established that any statement made without prior Miranda warnings is automatically inadmissible in court.
Section 66 of the IT Act requires the prosecution to prove that the accused acted 'dishonestly' or 'fraudulently' as defined in the Indian Penal Code.
Body corporates under Section 43A are required to publish their privacy policies and make them accessible to users before collection of sensitive personal data.
The Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination applies to civil proceedings in the same way as criminal proceedings.
Section 67B of the IT Act is consistent with India's obligations under the UNCRC Optional Protocol on the sale of children.
